subject: Accounting
title: Separation of Duties
description: A quick win: understand Separation of Duties.

hook.text: One employee writes checks, another approves them, a third reconciles the bank. That's the point.

buildup.text: Separation of duties ensures no single person controls an entire transaction from start to finish.

discovery.text: When duties are split, committing fraud requires collusion—which dramatically increases the risk of getting caught.

twist.text: Small businesses struggle with this—fewer employees means duties often overlap dangerously.

climax.text: In small teams, compensating controls like owner reviews or surprise audits can fill the gap.

punchline.text: Split the work. Split the risk.

quiz.question: Why is separation of duties important?
options: It prevents one person from controlling an entire transaction
It reduces the number of employees needed

details.summary: Separation of duties is a core internal control principle that divides critical financial tasks among different people so that no single individual can authorize, record, and have custody of assets — preventing both fraud and undetected errors.
details.whyItMatters: Separation of duties is arguably the most fundamental fraud prevention control. When one person handles everything — from approving payments to reconciling accounts — the opportunity for misappropriation skyrockets.
takeaways: No single person should authorize transactions, record them, and have custody of related assets
Separation creates a natural system of checks where one person's work is verified by another
Small organizations struggling with separation can use compensating controls like management reviews

faq.question: How does separation of duties prevent fraud?
faq.answer: If the person who approves vendor payments differs from who records them and who reconciles the bank, committing and concealing fraud requires collusion among multiple people. This dramatically reduces risk compared to one person handling everything.

faq.question: What if a company is too small to separate all duties?
faq.answer: Small businesses often can't achieve ideal separation with limited staff. They can implement compensating controls instead — such as owner review of bank statements, mandatory vacation policies (so someone else covers), surprise audits, and management approval of all transactions above a threshold.
